title: Users and their problems
summary: Every good product starts with a real person and a real pain. Learn to see both clearly.

lessons.title: Who is the user?
teach: A user is the person who uses the product. A customer is the person who pays. Sometimes they are the same person, sometimes not.
On Swiggy the person ordering is both user and customer. On Google Search you are the user, but advertisers are the customers who pay.
Many products have two or more sides. Uber has riders and drivers. Both are users, and the product must work for both.

questions.prompt: On YouTube, who pays most of the money?
questions.explain: Most viewers watch for free. Advertisers pay to show ads, and YouTube shares part of that money with creators.

questions.prompt: The user and the customer are always the same person.
questions.explain: On Instagram you are the user but brands buying ads are the customer. On a kids app the child uses it and the parent pays.

questions.prompt: Match each product to its two main sides.
questions.explain: Each is a marketplace. It only works when both sides show up, so the PM must think about both.

questions.prompt: One of these lines mixes up user and customer. Which one?
lines: Slack: the team uses it, the company pays
Google Search: you search, advertisers pay
Netflix: the viewer watches and the viewer pays
Gmail: advertisers use it, you pay
questions.explain: In free Gmail, you are the user and you do not pay. Google earns from ads and from paid Workspace plans for companies.

questions.prompt: For a school app like Byju's, who often decides to buy?
questions.explain: The child learns, but the parent pays. So the sales story speaks to parents about marks and the future.

questions.prompt: Put the steps to understand a new product's users in order.
steps: List everyone who touches the product
Mark who uses it and who pays
Talk to a few of them
questions.explain: First see everyone, then sort them, then focus, then learn from real people.

questions.prompt: A PM should care about drivers on Uber even though they are not paying for rides.
questions.explain: Without enough drivers, riders wait too long and leave. Both sides decide if the marketplace works.

lessons.title: Personas: picturing the user
teach: A persona is a short, made up picture of a typical user: who they are, what they want, and what gets in the way.
A good persona is based on real research, not guesses. It has a goal and a pain, not just age and city.
Most products have 2 or 3 key personas. Trying to please everyone usually pleases no one.

questions.prompt: Which persona is most useful for a PM?
options: Riya, 26, works late and wants dinner in under 30 minutes without cooking
questions.explain: It has a goal (dinner fast) and a pain (no time to cook). That is what helps you design features.

questions.prompt: A persona should be based on talking to real users.
questions.explain: Personas made from guesses often describe the team, not the user. Short interviews keep them honest.

questions.prompt: Match each persona to the product that fits them best.

pairs.left: A student saving for a phone
A shop owner taking digital payments
A traveller wanting a cheap stay

questions.explain: Each product solves a clear job for a clear type of person.

questions.prompt: One line in this persona does not help design. Which one?
lines: Goal: book a train ticket in 2 minutes
Pain: Tatkal tickets sell out fast
Fact: uses a cheap Android phone with slow internet
questions.explain: Favourite movie does not change what you build. Phone type and slow internet do, for an app like IRCTC or ixigo.

questions.prompt: Why do teams limit themselves to 2 or 3 key personas?
options: Focus: you can make a few people very happy
More personas cost money to print
questions.explain: Focus wins. Early Instagram focused on people sharing nice photos fast, not on every kind of social user.

questions.prompt: Put these parts of a persona in the order you would write them.
steps: Who they are in one line
What they are trying to get done
What gets in their way today
questions.explain: Who, then the goal, then the pain, then the current workaround, which is the thing you must beat.

questions.prompt: If two personas want opposite things, you must always build for both equally.
questions.explain: You often pick one as the main persona. Tinder, for example, designs mainly for quick casual swiping, not long profile reading.

lessons.title: Finding the real problem
teach: Users tell you what they want, but a PM looks for the problem behind it. People asked for faster horses; the problem was getting somewhere quickly.
A simple trick is to ask 'why?' a few times until you reach the real pain.
A problem is worth solving when it happens often, hurts a lot, and people already try to fix it.

questions.prompt: A user says 'add a dark mode to the banking app'. What is a good first question?
options: When do you use the app and what bothers you?
questions.explain: Maybe they check balance at night and the screen hurts their eyes. Knowing the real moment helps you solve it well.

questions.prompt: Put the 'ask why' chain in order for 'I want food delivered faster'.
steps: Why? Because I order when I'm already hungry
Why? Because I forget to plan meals
Real problem: no easy way to plan meals ahead
questions.explain: Each 'why' digs deeper. Now ideas like scheduled orders or meal plans appear, not just faster riders.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 signs that a problem is worth solving.
options: It hurts a lot when it happens
People already pay or hack around it
A competitor has a nice logo
questions.explain: Frequent, painful, and already being worked around. That is why UPI took off: paying small amounts was frequent and cash was a pain.

questions.prompt: If users already use messy workarounds, that is a good sign the problem is real.
questions.explain: Before Splitwise, friends used notes and Excel to split bills. The workaround proved the pain.

questions.prompt: Which line is a solution, not a problem?
lines: I lose track of who owes me money
I can never find a free slot with my doctor
I need a chatbot in the app
My parcel arrives when I'm not home
questions.explain: A chatbot is one possible answer. The problem behind it might be 'I can't get help quickly'.

questions.prompt: Match each product to the problem it solves.

pairs.right: Hard to find and book a good doctor
Finding a trusted plumber or cleaner

questions.explain: Each one started from a pain that was frequent and annoying.

questions.prompt: What does 'jobs to be done' mean?
options: A list of tasks for the PM
The progress a user is trying to make when they 'hire' a product
questions.explain: People 'hire' Zepto to get forgotten groceries fast, not because they love apps. Thinking in jobs keeps you focused on the outcome.

lessons.title: User journeys and pain points
teach: A user journey is every step a person takes to get something done, from first hearing about you to coming back again.
At each step, look for pain points: moments of confusion, waiting, or worry. These are where users quit.
Fixing the biggest drop off step often does more than adding a new feature.

questions.prompt: Put a first time food order on Swiggy in order.
questions.explain: Mapping the steps lets you ask where people get stuck, for example at payment.

questions.prompt: In a journey, 80% of users add to cart but only 30% pay. Where should you look first?
questions.explain: The biggest drop is between cart and payment. Surprise fees or failed payments are common causes.

questions.prompt: A user journey ends the moment the user pays.
questions.explain: It continues: delivery, eating, rating, and coming back. Repeat use is where most of the value is.

questions.prompt: Which of these is not a pain point?
lines: Hidden delivery fee shown only at the end
OTP takes two minutes to arrive
Order arrives 5 minutes early and hot
No way to change the address after ordering
questions.explain: Early and hot is a happy moment. The others make users worried or annoyed.

questions.prompt: Match each pain point to a likely fix.

pairs.left: Users don't trust a new seller

pairs.right: Send a reminder with one tap to continue
Offer UPI and save the last method

questions.explain: A good fix targets the exact reason people stop.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 steps that directly decide if a new Uber rider finishes a first trip.
options: Gets a driver within a few minutes
questions.explain: These are steps inside the journey. Ads and social follows may bring people in, but don't decide if the trip happens.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to find real pain points?
options: Watch real users try the product and read their complaints
questions.explain: Watching 5 users try your app usually shows the big problems. App store reviews are a free source too.
